lesson.title: From One Slope to Every Slope at Once
lesson.summary: Generalizes point-by-point derivative computations into a single derivative function by leaving the input symbolic, then verifies the resulting formula against earlier point-specific answers.
lesson.body:
Computing f prime of a one point at a time works, but it is repetitive: the algebra for f prime of 2, f prime of 3, and f prime of 10 on the same function follows an identical pattern with only the number changing. The derivative function collapses all of those individual computations into a single formula by leaving the input as a variable, typically x, instead of a fixed number a. The result, written f prime of x, is a new function in its own right: feed it any input, and it returns the slope of the tangent line to f at that input.

The definition is the same limit as before, just with a replaced by the variable x: f prime of x equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(x + h) minus f(x)] divided by h. Since x is now a placeholder rather than a specific number, the algebra has to be done symbolically, but the payoff is a formula that works for every point at once.

Work through f(x) = x cubed in general. f prime of x equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [(x + h) cubed minus x cubed] divided by h. Expanding (x + h) cubed using the binomial pattern gives x cubed plus 3 x squared h plus 3 x h squared plus h cubed. Subtracting x cubed leaves 3 x squared h plus 3 x h squared plus h cubed, and every remaining term has a factor of h, so dividing by h gives 3 x squared plus 3 x h plus h squared. Now let h approach 0: the terms containing h vanish, leaving f prime of x equals 3 x squared.

Check this against earlier work: plugging x = 2 into 3 x squared gives 3 times 4, which is 12, exactly the value found for f prime of 2 by direct substitution in the limit definition section. The general formula and the point by point computation agree, as they must, since the general formula is nothing more than the same computation done before fixing a number. The same consistency shows up with f(x) = x squared: earlier tangent slope computations found f prime of x equals 2x, so at x = 3 that gives 6, matching the tangent line built at the very start of this sequence, and the position function s(t) = 5 t squared had derivative 10t, which at t = 2 gives 20, matching the instantaneous velocity found earlier.

The same generalization works just as well starting from f(x) = x squared. Redoing the limit with a variable x instead of a fixed input: f prime of x equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [(x + h) squared minus x squared] divided by h, and expanding (x + h) squared gives x squared plus 2xh plus h squared, so subtracting x squared and dividing by h leaves 2x plus h, which approaches 2x as h approaches 0. That confirms, symbolically this time rather than just by matching numbers, that f prime of x equals 2x for every x, not only at the specific point x = 3 used earlier.

A pattern is emerging across these examples, power 2 gives a derivative with a leading 2, power 3 gives a leading 3, but resist the urge to treat that as proven from only two cases; it becomes a formal rule, the power rule, only after being established properly with the same limit machinery used here. For now the important shift is conceptual: the derivative is not just a number attached to one point, it is a function that can be evaluated anywhere, and having it in hand means never repeating the limit computation for that function again.
